opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot about a particular scenario that I find pretty plausible: the people building the most powerful AI systems are under intense competitive pressure, they're moving fast, and they're not going to be very willing to make big sacrifices for safety. I sometimes call this the "rushed, unreasonable developer" world. Maybe there's a race between a few companies, or between the US and China, and everyone feels that if they slow down by six months, someone less careful will get there first.

In that world, the question isn't "what's the ideal set of safety measures?" It's "what will actually get implemented?" And the answer is heavily determined by cost. If a technique makes your model 20% worse on capability benchmarks, or doubles your inference bill, or requires a year of extra research before deployment, it's very hard to get a company in a tight race to adopt it. Even well-intentioned leadership will face internal pushback: "our competitors aren't doing this, why are we handicapping ourselves?"

Whereas if you can say, "here's a set of control measures: trusted monitoring, some auditing of suspicious actions, restrictions on what the model can access, and it costs you a few percent of compute and barely touches the product," that's a much easier sell. It's the kind of thing a safety team can push through without needing the CEO to make a heroic decision.

There's also a more structural point. A lot of what I care about is reducing risk from models that might be scheming against us, models that are actively trying to undermine our safety measures. You want measures that hold up even if the model is adversarial. But if those measures are expensive, they'll get cut the moment there's pressure, and the moment of maximal pressure is plausibly exactly when the models are most dangerous. So cheapness is part of what makes a technique robust in practice, not just on paper.

And finally, low cost makes things easier to coordinate on or regulate. If you're asking a government or an industry agreement to mandate something, it's much more realistic to mandate measures that don't impose huge competitive costs. So I think a lot of the highest-leverage safety work right now is figuring out how to get most of the risk reduction for a small fraction of the cost. That's a big part of why I'm excited about AI control as a research direction.

r001.rationale: It says costly measures face internal pushback and may require the CEO to make a “heroic decision,” explaining how limited company buy-in constrains what costs safety techniques can impose.

r002.rationale: It mentions capability losses and added research time as reasons companies may reject a technique, but does not say that reduced AI productivity could slow alignment research performed by those AIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic argument is that safety techniques only help if they actually get used, and whether they get used depends a lot on what they cost. The way I think about it, the people who are going to be deploying these models are AI companies that are under a lot of competitive pressure, and if you come to them with a technique that says, "You can make your model safer, but it's going to be 30% worse at the thing you care about, or it's going to cost you three times as much compute to run," there's a very real chance they just won't do it. Or they'll do it halfheartedly, or they'll do it for the first deployment and then quietly stop when it gets annoying.

So when we think about what we're trying to do with AI control, a lot of the design constraint is: can we come up with something where the overhead is low enough that it's basically a no-brainer to adopt? Like, if you can get a big reduction in the probability of catastrophe for a few percent of your inference compute and almost no hit to capabilities, that's the kind of thing that a lab's safety team can actually push through internally. Whereas if the cost is huge, you're relying on the lab making a big sacrifice, and I'm just not that optimistic that those sacrifices happen reliably across all the actors who matter.

There's also a more subtle point, which is that the cheaper your techniques are, the more layers of them you can stack. A lot of the safety stories I find most plausible involve a bunch of different measures that are each individually imperfect — monitoring, auditing some fraction of actions, restricting what the model can do in certain contexts — and the combined effect is what gets you somewhere good. But you can only stack a bunch of measures if each one is cheap. If every measure cost you a lot, you'd have to pick one, and that one thing is probably not enough on its own.

And then the last thing I'd say is that I think being honest about costs is important for the field's credibility. There's a bit of a tendency in safety research to propose things that would be great if everyone adopted them, without really grappling with why they wouldn't. I'd rather we design for the world we're actually in, where people are going to be making these trade-offs under pressure, and try to make the safe option also the easy option.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure may lead companies to reject costly safety measures, but it does not explain that limited political capital within a company constrains acceptable costs.

r002.rationale: The response mentions possible capability and compute costs, but does not connect reduced AI productivity to slower alignment research performed by those AIs.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that we want people to actually use them. A safety technique can work really well in principle, but if it makes your AI system ten times more expensive, or substantially less useful, then people have a strong incentive to skip it or find some cheaper substitute that might not work as well.

There are two kinds of costs here. One is the direct cost: how much extra compute or human oversight do you need? The other is how much capability you give up. Does the technique prevent you from using the system for some of the tasks that made you want to build it in the first place?

And this matters even if the people deploying the system care quite a lot about safety. They still face tradeoffs, and they might be competing with people who are willing to take more risks. If we can make a safety measure cheap and preserve most of the system’s usefulness, adopting it becomes a much easier decision.

So I don’t think the technical goal should just be ‘find a procedure that makes the system safe.’ We should also ask, ‘How burdensome is this procedure, and will people have good reasons to follow it?’ Lowering those costs makes technical progress more likely to translate into actual safety.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deployment tradeoffs and competition, but does not mention limited political capital within an AI company constraining acceptable safety costs.

r002.rationale: It says safety techniques can make systems less useful, but does not explain that reduced AI productivity can slow alignment research performed by those AIs.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that we need people to actually use them. It’s not enough to come up with a technique that makes an AI system safer if using it makes the system much less useful or much more expensive.

Imagine you have two ways of deploying an AI. One is safer, but it costs twice as much and gets substantially worse results. Even if a company would prefer to deploy safely, there’s going to be a lot of pressure to choose the cheaper, more capable option, especially if its competitors are doing that. Whereas if the safety measures cost a few percent and barely affect performance, adopting them is a much easier decision.

So I think part of the technical problem is finding safety measures that impose small enough costs that people are willing to use them. You can also try to change the incentives through policy, but that’s easier when the thing you’re asking people to do is cheap.

r001.rationale: The response discusses company pressure to choose cheaper, more capable systems, but does not explain that limited political capital within an AI company constrains acceptable safety costs.
